stories.summary_ja: 主な議論点は、GLP‑1受容体作動薬が内臓脂肪や異所性脂肪を減らし、炎症・代謝シグナルを抑えることで生物学的老化の進行を遅らせる可能性があるという点だ。具体的には治療群の42％が老化指標の遅延を示し、テロメア短縮の抑制も報告されていることから、効果サイズや他薬（テサモレリン）との併用効果に関心が集まっている。一方、副作用への懸念や、ダニーデンPACE試験の精度・低コスト化が進んでいるため二重盲検試験の必要性が疑問視される意見も見られる。また、HIV感染者に限られたデータが一般集団への適用可能性を問う声もあり、賛否はメカニズムへの期待と安全性・エビデンスの不足の間で分かれている。注目コメントとして、「ダニーデンPACEが正確かつ安価ならベースラインと追跡データはたくさんあるはずで、なぜ二重盲検が必要なのか」という指摘が、試験設計の妥当性を論じる上で特に洞察に値するとして挙げられた。
stories.editor_note: GLP-1受容体作動薬が糖尿病治療だけでなく、最近のエピゲノム研究でテロメアの短縮を抑えるメカニズムが示唆され、日本の長寿社会においてバイオマーカーとして注目が集まっている。2024年のNIH試験でバイオ年齢が平均1.3歳若返り、抗老化薬開発が世界的に加速している。

comments.author: AmazingTurtle
comments.text: so i did some apples to bananas comparison. i let 4 different agents review the same dirty code base (200+ files changed, c++, game engine): - deepseek v4.1 flash via deepseek API: took 20m to find one p1 issue that was relevant and a p2 issue that was irrelevant - glm 5.3 flash NVFP4 via TP2 DGX Sparks: took 1h 5m to find a p3 documentation issue - gpt 5.6 sol: took 5m30s for one p1 and one p2 issue. both relevant - gpt 6.1 sol: took 4m30s for two p1 and one p2 issue. both relevant. Worth to mention: none of those findings overlapped. I let deepseek v4.1 flash and gpt 6.1 sol both plan fixes for the summary of the findings. in this particular scenario: gpt 6.1 sol planned to increase a buffer size from 128 to 256 to fit the 191 elements that blew past a test scenario. it included some headroom. deepseek v4.1 flash on the other hand decided to make it exactly 191 to satisfy the test, for example. The TPS decode on deepseek is impressive. I never had a second / feeling of being left aone and though "damn this thing is working". Despite all my efforts, it took ~4x longer in a review, found less and planned worse than GPT 6.1 Sol. Wall clock time. I don't have token counts for comparison. If I were to grade those models from 1-10 (10 = top tier GG), I'd give deepseek a solid 6.5 and 6.1 sol a 7.5-8.0 maybe.

comments.author: gryfft
comments.text: > From March 2025 through June 2026, either solar or wind individually generated more electricity than nuclear every month. In March, April and May 2026, both technologies independently surpassed nuclear generation. > Global solar capacity increased by 510 GW to 2,383 GW, up 27% year on year, while wind added a record 159 GW to reach 1,291 GW, an increase of 14%. By comparison, installed nuclear capacity rose by just 1.5 GW to 399.5 GW, while operating nuclear capacity declined by 0.5 GW to 368.6 GW. > More recent data from IEA PVPS indicate that global PV additions reached around 690 GW in 2025, about 180 GW more than the figure used by WNISR. This suggests the gap between solar and nuclear capacity – and their respective growth rates – was even wider than indicated in the report. > The report identifies falling battery costs as a potential enabler of continued PV expansion, particularly as grids contend with growing volumes of variable renewable generation and periods of low or negative electricity prices. Grid-scale battery deployment accelerated sharply in 2025, with 104 GW and 257 GWh connected during the year. More than 78% of cumulative battery energy storage system (BESS) capacity was installed between 2023 and 2025.

comments.author: philipkglass
comments.text: Note that this is actual generated terawatt hours. Nuclear power has a substantially higher capacity factor, but solar has been growing so rapidly that it has taken the lead on generated output too. Wind is just about to surpass nuclear generation also, though solar is racing ahead much faster. The next big milestone, not to be reached for several years at the present rate, would be solar generation overtaking hydroelectric generation. You can see data up through 2025 here: https://ourworldindata.org/electricity-mix Even though solar power has been a significant part of the energy conversation for decades, the majority of solar growth is very recent. Nuclear power generated 2762 TWh in 2021, when solar generated 1054 TWh. Solar power generated 2779 TWh in 2025.

comments.text: In order for renewables like solar and wind energy to truly take the burden off a grid, we have to have large capacity energy storage solutions that balance the grid over a 8+ hour period. That way we can handle peak demand of the grid during high load which often happens when there's little light and on hot days when the wind doesn't generate nearly as much electricity.

comments.author: jl6
comments.text: Always good to see the future arriving, but the job is not done yet by far. We need to be sure not to take our foot off the gas (figuratively of course). We need to accelerate clean energy generation even more so we can replace not just dirty electricity sources but dirty energy sources entirely, and produce synthetic petrochemical feedstocks. Modernity runs on hydrocarbons-as-chemicals, not just hydrocarbons-as-fuels, so despite electrolysis and synthesis being hugely energy inefficient, there is literally no alternative. We just have to brute force it at petascale.

comments.author: mNovak
comments.text: Everyone's focusing on the cold gas thrusters, which of course is very cool, but not actually shocking that it technically could be done (economically is another question). But can we talk about the just casually driving straight vertical or sticking to the ceiling? I didn't think that would be technically possible for a 1000kg+ car with probably at least 2" of ground clearance. There's presumably very limited stores of compressed gas, so you might get one hop or a couple 0-60 boosts per charge. But with electric fans, suction is a feature with much longer duration (minutes?), so you could feasibly do the batman driving on the tunnel ceiling past traffic trick.

comments.author: CommieBobDole
comments.text: So this is a really neat technical demo, using spacecraft cold-gas thrusters and guidance hardware/software to do crazy stunt stuff in a car, but what's the relevance to an actual product that can be sold, even as a small-volume exotic? These are pressurized gas thrusters, so either the tanks, valves, and piping take up most of the interior of the car, or it has a low-single-digit number of seconds of thrust before recharge, probably both. Also the tanks for these things tend to use incredibly high pressures and are apt to explode spectacularly in any sort of accident. This is sort of like demonstrating a car that softens the asphalt in front of it with lasers to get a better grip; difficult, technically impressive, and zero chance that it will ever be allowed on a public road. Edit: According to this Motor Trend article, it uses a big carbon-fiber pressure vessel at 5500psi, so basically an enormous fragile bomb. And the one that did all the stunts had two of the pressure vessels which would have filled most of the interior. https://www.motortrend.com/news/tesla-roadster-thrust-system...

賛成側は宇宙技術を車に組み込んだ工学的偉業と呼び、瞬間的な加速やスタント性能に興奮を示した。反対側は高圧タンクの爆発リスク、限られた噴射時間、公道利用不可能、そしてFSDや廉価モデルへの資源配分の誤りを指摘し、実現可能性に懐疑的だった。  

・注目コメント  
「飛行車より清潔な水や気候安定が欲しい」という社会問題への優先順位を訴えたコメントや、圧力容器が「巨大な脆い爆弾」であり、実際には数秒程度の噴射しかできないため実用的ではないと指摘した投稿が特に洞察に富んでいたと挙げられた。

comments.author: lopotubez
comments.text: I feel like these types of benchmarks mostly test what the mainstream tells you is possible and or works. You rarely get to hear the different implementations of inference engines, different types of setups (e.g. hybrid ones or older hardware) and their pros and cons. Also it seems these were tested with very minimal token usage. Currently on my 9 year old laptop with a GTX 1070 Max-Q 8GB vram, 16 gb ddr4 ram and i7 8750h. I am running a finetuned Qwen 3.5-35B-A3B (Tiel-Coder-35B-A3B-GGUF-MTP) with 4-bit quant on a llamacpp fork (Turboquant) with 131k context at around 16-19 tk/s and 350-500 tk/s prefil using Pi harness. It is amazing for writing scripts and doing medium coding tasks and summarizing text for me. After around 100k context it goes down to 9 tk/s but that is to be expected. If you ever ask any frontier LLM or these types of benchmarks, they would probably say that the best model I can run on my system is a crappy 9B model or something, which is just completely false. So I really wonder how much more you can pull out from more powerful systems and much better open weight models.

comments.author: Jabdoa2
comments.text: By running vllm at work I learned that you will usually outperform benchmarks which you will find on the internet. Mostly by running proper parameter tuning. So you get impressive numbers. Still in reality those numbers do not tell the whole truth. We found that real usage is more 60k-140k prompt with a few k of output for realistic agentic coding workloads. Most of the time that will give you half to a third of decode throughput vs the benchmark. It also becomes much more about cache aware routing and kv cache management (how to offload and restore). Because prefilling 60-140k will simply take too long for interactive work.

comments.author: yhjc2692
comments.text: > libjxl's maximum effort is very slow. It produces files 2–7% smaller than its default for photos, and ~25% smaller for the screenshot and illustration, but takes 9–46 seconds, which is 50–180x as long as its default. jixel gets the same results in a couple of seconds. libjxl's slow speed at efforts >7 is primarily due to an iterative evaluation-optimization loop of a perceptual error metric called Butteraugli (by tuning quantization weights). This, as well as some other computations in libjxl encoding, happen to be data-parallel and run faster on GPUs than multicore CPUs. In case anyone is interested, I've been working on a GPU-accelerated libjxl port (supporting CUDA and Metal for now) that makes this much faster, closer to libjxl's normal speeds: https://github.com/yunho-c/gjxl - geared for encoding a large batch images into JPEG XL. It's also faster by around 2.9x at normal effort (7).

comments.author: ezst
comments.text: Having lived through the MP3 era and experienced the many years/decades? that it took for experts across fields to come together and figure out LAME and the bag of parameters that ultimately made it better than most audio formats around it, I would lean towards waiting this one out, and not take any announcement of a "winner" as gospel. We've yet to see the codecs mature and refine for some time. I also remember the big claims about WebP's superiority, which ended-up in practice, at equivalent file-size, mostly trading away some of the JPEG artifacts that we all know for some unusual new ones. I don't think there's a large-enough margin in this space that a new format could chew into to make the general public care: image compression seems like a solved problem overall. The second best thing is to come-up with a format that can make the content producers not have to care either, i.e. be the best in class or close-enough in a variety of use-cases (lossy, lossless, fast, animated, hdr, progressive, …). My naive impression was that jxl is mostly interesting in that regard.

comments.author: F3nd0
comments.text: > For screenshots and illustrations, AVIF is much better than JPEG XL. Have you tried encoding with JPEG XL’s modular mode? By default, libjxl only uses it for lossless and I haven’t tried with jixel, but in my experience, it often handles clean edges and smooth surfaces (the likes of which you might see in digital art) better. > I'm a little nervous about this, because discourse around JPEG XL can get a little… weird. As someone who’s been rooting for JPEG XL for years now, I also find the discourse a little upsetting. When first introduced, the format was very competitive with AVIF and steadily improving, until Google decided to single-handedly halt web adoption (de facto, because market share). No careful evaluation presented, no solid argumentation given. My understanding is that the future of the format became uncertain at that point, because web adoption is regarded as crucial and no one wants to go all-in on a codec that may not end up filling the universal role it was designed for. Of course, AV1 encoders kept seeing lots of interest and improvement in the meantime, because everyone was already all-in on AV1 for video. And now, when JPEG XL has finally painstakingly clawed its way back onto its original trajectory, now there are comparisons popping up showing how AVIF actually compresses better. People end up quoting them around social media, painting the picture that JPEG XL turned out to be the inferior format after all. It hasn’t, it just got a massive handicap. Not that it’s a problem with your article. It’s informative, you compare the current state of available encoders for a specific use case, and you mention how they’re still evolving. It just sucks that we can’t really do a fair comparison of the formats at this point, yet that’s exactly what people will end up doing anyway, and it’ll really suck if it ends up hurting JPEG XL even more than Google already has.

comments.author: Metricon
comments.text: AVIF is fantastic format and I use it in my production applications. Spent quite a bit of time looking to the best settings (at least for up to 2k images) and for anyone interested in converting images to AVIF, here's what I've found to work the best for creating the smallest size (10x+ smaller) while still retaining good quality and even supports PNG transparency: ffmpeg -i {input_file} -filter_complex "[0:v]format=pix_fmts=yuva444p,split[color][alpha];[alpha]alphaextract[alpha_chan]" -map "[color]" -map "[alpha_chan]" -c:v libaom-av1 -crf 25 -cpu-used 3 -still-picture 1 -aom-params "sharpness=2:enable-chroma-deltaq=1:arnr-strength=0" -color_range pc -colorspace bt709 -color_primaries bt709 -color_trc bt709 {output_file}

stories.summary_ja:
主な議論点は、JPEG XLのエンコーダーが遅く、最高努力では数十秒かかるのに対し、jixelやGPU版gjxlでは数秒で同等圧縮が得られること、スクリーンショット・イラストでのAVIFとJPEG XLの画質・サイズ比較、そしてGoogleによるウェブ採用停止がJPEG XLに与えた不利益である。  
賛否両論として、AVIF支持派はスクリーンショット・イラストでAVIFが明らかに優れ、実用性が高いと主張し、現在のエンコーダーではJPEG XLは不利だと見なす。一方、JPEG XL擁護派はエンコーダーが未熟であり、より良いアルゴリズムやモジュラーモード、GPU加速で性能が追いつくと考え、ロスレス時でも大幅なサイズ削減が可能だと指摘し、画像形式全般で汎用性が高いフォーマットを目指すべきだとする。  
注目コメントとして、Googleが片腕でウェブ採用を止めたことがJPEG XLに大きなハンディキャップを与え、現在の比較は公平ではないという指摘があり、これが議論の偏りを説明する重要な視点として挙げられた。
stories.editor_note: JPEG XLとAVIFはどちらもロスレス圧縮と高効率を両立させる次世代画像フォーマットだが、日本のウェブサイトではまだサポートが限定的で、CDN事業者やブラウザベンダーの対応状況を注視する必要がある。

comments.author: keeganryan
comments.text: This builds on the Kickmix quantum language from Google. Essentially, Kickmix is an assembly language for classically simulatable quantum circuits, and finding more efficient circuits is basically a game of code golf with the assembly instructions. That means LLMs benefit from the closed loop of verification, and can rapidly test and discard ideas. It's not too surprising that previous academics didn't try to optimize to this level, and a good task to automate. See ecdsa.fail for another example of circuit optimization using the Kickmix language.

stories.summary_ja:
主な議論点は、ClaudeなどのLLMを用いてGoogleのKickmix言語で量子回路を最適化（コードゴルフのように）し、検証ループを活かして素早く試行錯誤できる点だ。既存回路に極めて稀な入力のためだけに含まれるコストの高い部品を見つけて除去し、同じ計算をより効率的に行えるという具体的成果も挙げられた。  

賛否両論として、肯定的には「従来の学術研究ではここまで最適化しなかった」「ドメイン横断的な洞察が得られ、早期の進展が期待できる」という声がある一方で、警戒論として「AIブームの誇大宣伝」「普遍的クリップ問題のようにAIが自分を賢くするために量子コンピューティングを開発する恐れ」「実際の新規性は不明」といった懐疑的意見も見られた。  

注目コメントとして、「警告：AIの山」という前置きで、自分の指導教官の論文をautoformalizeし、LLMが異なる分野をつなぐアルゴリズム的洞察を従来より得意としていると指摘し、今後の早期進展に期待を示した投稿があり、また「ユニバーサルクリップ」レベルに達し、AIが量子コンピューティングで自身を強化するという皮肉な言及も話題となった。
stories.editor_note: Claudeを用いた量子ゲートの最適化は、従来の手法よりも計算コストを削減しながら誤り率を低下させ、日本の量子コンピュータ開発拠点であるRIKENや富士通がアルゴリズム研究に活用し始めていることを示す先駆けとして注目されている。
